lesson.title: Adjective Agreement
lesson.subtitle: Descriptive adjectives following the noun: -o/-a/-os/-as patterns

hook.title: Painting the Noun First, Coloring It Second
hook.content: In English, you hold the color in your head before naming the object: 'a white house'. In Spanish, you put the object on the canvas first and then brush the description onto it: una casa blanca ('a house white'), un libro nuevo ('a book new'), un café negro ('a coffee black')!

pattern.title: The Four-Corner Agreement Grid: -o, -a, -os, -as
pattern.content: Adjectives ending in -o have four forms: blanco (m.sg.), blanca (f.sg.), blancos (m.pl.), blancas (f.pl.). Adjectives ending in -e (verde, grande) or a consonant (azul, natural) have just TWO forms — singular and plural! Wait: how do you make a plural in Spanish? If a word ends in a vowel, add -s (casas, verdes); if it ends in a consonant, add -es (hoteles, azules)!
pattern.linguist_note: Post-nominal adjective placement is the unmarked Romance order for distinguishing/restrictive attributes.
pattern.trap_note: Notice that plural of el is LOS (not *eles!) and plural of la is LAS: el libro → los libros, la casa → las casas.

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: la casa blanca, el café negro, el libro nuevo, la ciudad hermosa, verde, azul
exercises.meaning: the white house, the black coffee, the new book, the beautiful city, green (invariable gender), blue (plural: azules)
exercises.explanation: Noun comes first; adjective agrees in gender and number.

exercises.prompt: Spanish 'hermoso' ('beautiful') evolved from Latin 'formōsus' ('finely shaped', with initial f- turning into silent h-!). What historical Portuguese name ('Beautiful Island') was given to Taiwan by 16th-century navigators?
exercises.meaning: Formosa (historical name of Taiwan) is the exact same word as Spanish hermosa!
exercises.explanation: Latin formōsus kept its f- in Portuguese Formosa and English 'form', and turned f- into silent h- in Spanish hermoso.

exercises.prompt: How do you form the plural of 'el hotel azul' ('the blue hotel' → 'the blue hotels')?
exercises.explanation: Masculine el becomes plural los; consonant-ending hotel and azul add -es: los hoteles azules.
Quiero + un café (masculine) + negro (after the noun).

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'Una casa blanca y nueva'?
exercises.meaning: A new white house (literal Spanish blueprint: A house white and new)
exercises.explanation: Spanish names the object first (una casa) and then layers its descriptions (blanca y nueva).

summary.outcome: Place descriptive adjectives after the noun and match them across singular/plural and masculine/feminine.

use_example.german: Tengo un libro nuevo y vivo en una casa blanca.
use_example.english: I have a new book and I live in a white house.

summary.takeaway: Vowel-ending words add -s in the plural (libros, casas); consonant-ending words add -es (hoteles, azules).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([1101] Noun-First Word Order): build noun-first descriptions across colors and qualities.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'The house is white and beautiful'
twist.target_answer: La casa es blanca y hermosa
twist.explanation: blanca and hermosa agree with feminine la casa.

foreshadow.line: Next in Topic 12: how to step into the future using ir a ('going to') + any infinitive.

payoff.text: Combine tener and hay from Topic 10 with post-nominal adjectives to describe everything you own or see.

casa.etymology_derivation: Latin casa originally meant a cottage, replacing domus in everyday Romance speech.

hotel.etymology_derivation: Silent initial H. Latin hospitāle gives both 'hospital' and 'hotel'.

verde.etymology_derivation: Ends in -e, so masculine and feminine are identical.

rojo.etymology_derivation: Latin russeus ('reddish') → rojo. Cognate with English russet and ruby.

azul.etymology_derivation: Hispano-Arabic lāzaward ('lapis lazuli') → azul. English azure is the exact same word.

hermoso.etymology_derivation: Latin formōsus ('finely formed') — initial f- became silent h-: hermoso!
